claim: Dorst and Cross 2001 is a protocol study of nine experienced industrial designers, with designs rated for quality and creativity, that tests a problem-solution co-evolution model.
quote: From the protocol data we identify aspects of creativity in design related to the formulation of the design problem and to the concept of originality.
title: Creativity in the design process: co-evolution of problem-solution
transfer: Abstract text came through a search summary, not an opened page (ORO page 403, PDF host unreachable). Treat as hypothesis: a frame-then-partial-solution bridge step, tested as an experiment arm only.

claim: Dorst and Cross propose default and surprise problem/solution spaces as refinements of the co-evolution model.
quote: We propose refinements to the co-evolution model, and suggest relevant new concepts of 'default' and 'surprise' problem/solution spaces.
title: Creativity in the design process: co-evolution of problem-solution
transfer: A surprise check: ask whether a partial solution reveals a frame the default frame missed.

claim: A 2026 scoping review of 16 DRS conference papers (2001-2025) finds the Dorst-Cross model widely used and developed, and says it was also critiqued, but the abstract does not say what the critiques are.
quote: revealing how the model has been adopted, developed, and critiqued.
authors: Michael Mose Biskjaer, Kim Halskov, Alwin de Rooij
title: Problem-solution co-evolution research in the DRS conference community (2001-2025)
transfer: none. Shows the model is a theory in wide use, not an empirically validated procedure. No replication with effect sizes was found.

claim: The same review finds problem and solution spaces are treated as distinct and interdependent, and suggests linking to psychological research on problem construction.
quote: We find that problem and solution spaces are considered distinct and interdependent.
authors: Michael Mose Biskjaer, Kim Halskov, Alwin de Rooij
title: Problem-solution co-evolution research in the DRS conference community (2001-2025)
transfer: Keep the frame record and the solution record separate, each updating the other.

claim: Kruger and Cross 2006 exists as 'Solution driven versus problem driven design: strategies and outcomes' in Design Studies. Bibliographic record confirmed via Crossref; abstract and results not opened.
title: Solution driven versus problem driven design: strategies and outcomes
transfer: none until the findings are read.

claim: Sio, Kotovsky and Cagan 2015 is titled a meta-analytic review of examples in design, in Design Studies. Title and venue confirmed via Crossref; abstract not retrieved.
authors: Ut Na Sio, Kenneth Kotovsky, Jonathan Cagan
title: Fixation or inspiration? A meta-analytic review of the role of examples on design processes
transfer: none until findings are read. The meta-analysis label is supported by the title; effect sizes are still unread.

claim: A short review of examples in design education concludes that fixation risk can be limited by managing quantity, abstraction, proximity and method of examples.
title: Examples in Design Education: Inspiration or Fixation?
transfer: When showing the agent lessons or examples, vary abstraction and distance, and test before versus after first generation.

claim: Chain-of-thought explanations can be plausible yet unfaithful: biasing features in the input shift answers, but the written reasoning omits them and often rationalizes the biased answer. Accuracy fell by up to 36 percent on BIG-Bench Hard with GPT-3.5 and Claude 1.0.
quote: CoT explanations can systematically misrepresent the true reason for a model's prediction.
authors: Miles Turpin, Julian Michael, Ethan Perez, Samuel R. Bowman
title: Language Models Don't Always Say What They Think: Unfaithful Explanations in Chain-of-Thought Prompting
transfer: A written problem frame may not be what drives the answer. Test it: swap the frame and check if the answer changes.

claim: Lanham et al. intervene on the written reasoning (add mistakes, paraphrase) and find models differ a lot across tasks in how much they condition on it; larger models tended to give less faithful reasoning on most tasks.
quote: Models show large variation across tasks in how strongly they condition on the CoT
title: Measuring Faithfulness in Chain-of-Thought Reasoning
transfer: Add a causal test for the frame step: corrupt or swap the frame and see whether the final answer moves. Quote is the fetch tool's rendering of the abstract, so check wording against the paper.

claim: LLM-as-judge for creativity is unreliable: it gives inconsistent verdicts under minor prompt changes and shows label bias.
quote: LLM-as-a-Judge producing inconsistent judgments under minor prompt variations and exhibiting bias towards particular labels.
authors: Li-Chun Lu, Miri Liu, Pin-Chun Lu, Yufei Tian, Shao-Hua Sun, Nanyun Peng
title: Rethinking Creativity Evaluation: A Critical Analysis of Existing Creativity Evaluations
transfer: Do not use one LLM score as the novelty signal. Use pairwise comparison with shuffled order, several prompts, and a non-LLM measure such as embedding distance or count of distinct answers.

claim: On multi-step creativity tasks LLM judges show verbosity and leniency bias, and wide scoring ranges make judgments less stable. Separating analysis from judging reduces this.
quote: LLM is susceptible to biases such as verbosity bias and leniency bias.
authors: Xiangyu Wang, Jin Wu, Xiaoyu Li, Chanjin Zheng, Yifeng Zhou
title: Decoupled Analysis-Judging: An Automated Creativity Evaluator Using LLMs in Complex Multi-step Creativity Tasks
transfer: Evaluator step: write analysis of each candidate first, then score on a narrow scale, and control for length.

claim: A 2026 paper reports that LLM judges are biased in creative literary translation (favor machine output, penalize creative choices). Known from a listing summary only.
title: Creativity Bias: How Machine Evaluation Struggles with Creativity in Literary Translations
transfer: Adjacent domain. Supports human-checked anchors for any judge.

claim: The Xu et al. agent preprint tested a plain loop, a self-regulation loop and a separate-agent co-regulation loop on one battery pack design problem. Both regulated loops beat the plain loop at no significant added cost, and co-regulation beat self-regulation.
quote: without significantly increasing the computational cost
authors: Zeda Xu, Nikolas Martelaro, Christopher McComb
title: Supervising Ralph Wiggum: Exploring a Metacognitive Co-Regulation Agentic AI Loop for Engineering Design
transfer: The only controlled LLM fixation-mitigation test found. One problem, so run it as an arm at equal tokens on our own tasks.

claim: In a 48-hour hackathon, ChatGPT 4.0 placed second of six teams, was strong at idea generation, but abandoned promising concepts early and showed design fixation.
title: ChatGPT as an inventor: Eliciting the strengths and weaknesses of current large language models against humans in engineering design
transfer: Add a persistence rule: do not drop a candidate until a concrete check fails.

claim: CHECK: Dorst and Cross 2001 co-evolution. Verdict: paper and abstract exist and the model is widely cited (scoping review of 16 DRS papers). Not verified: effect sizes, replications, or any LLM test. Still a hypothesis for agent design. Full text not opened.
transfer: Keep M2 as an experiment arm.

claim: CHECK: Kruger and Cross 2006 'no strategy predicts better outcomes'. Verdict: UNSETTLED. Citation confirmed, findings not opened, so the earlier claim stays memory-only.
transfer: none

claim: CHECK: Sio et al. 2015 is a meta-analysis. Verdict: label supported by the title; effect sizes unread. Jansson and Smith 1991 was not re-opened (no source retrieved), so it stays memory-only, credibility cap 50.
transfer: none

claim: CHECK: Mullen 1991 / Diehl-Stroebe production blocking. Verdict: UNSETTLED. No source retrieved (search budget exhausted, Crossref rate limited, PubMed empty, guessed DOI 404). The nominal-group claim stays memory-only.
transfer: Testable directly: compare independent parallel calls pooled versus one interacting multi-turn session at equal tokens.

claim: CHECK: does a written frame causally change an LLM answer. Verdict: PARTLY. Turpin and Lanham show written reasoning is often not the true cause and that dependence varies by task. A frame step must be tested by intervention on our tasks, not assumed. No direct test of problem-frame text found.
transfer: Frame-swap ablation as a benchmark control.

claim: CHECK: LLM-as-judge bias for novelty. Verdict: SUPPORTED as a risk by two fetched preprints (verbosity, leniency, label bias, prompt sensitivity). No peer-reviewed meta-analysis found; search budget ran out.
transfer: Never rely on one LLM judge for the novelty signal.

claim: CHECK: LLM agent design fixation mitigation controlled test. Verdict: one found (Xu 2026, 1 problem, preprint). The equal-token advantage stays single-source.
transfer: Run as an arm.
